FINANCIAL ANALYTICS / ML

CASE STUDY / 02

Finding the rare signal in financial noise.

A rare-event classification study of approximately 9.5 million transactions—and an investigation into why impressive model scores can be misleading.

01 / THE QUESTION

The business context.

In financial transaction monitoring, the events that matter are rare. A model can achieve high accuracy while missing almost every suspicious transaction. The analytical challenge is to evaluate detection quality without hiding behind a reassuring headline score.

02 / EXPLORE THE WORK

RARE EVENTS. REAL QUESTIONS.
0.104%Laundering-labeled records
Conceptual illustration

THE EVALUATION QUESTION

Which metric deserves attention?

The majority-class trap

With a positive rate of 0.104%, an all-negative classifier would be about 99.896% accurate and detect zero positive cases. This is a class-distribution calculation, not a reported model result.

Conceptual evaluation guide. No model performance is simulated.

03 / THE APPROACH

From question to evidence.

01

Explore

Studied the scale of class imbalance and the distribution of laundering-labeled transactions.

02

Compare

Compared baseline and classification models, including tree-based methods and logistic regression.

03

Evaluate

Examined class weighting and thresholds, focusing on precision, recall, and PR-AUC rather than accuracy alone.

04

Challenge

Investigated near-perfect performance by testing the removal of Laundering_type, a feature that could expose the target label.

04 / WHAT I LEARNED

The useful part of the analysis.

01

Accuracy is insufficient

Only about 0.104% of records carry the positive label. Class imbalance makes overall accuracy a poor headline measure.

02

Question perfect results

Removing a potentially leaking feature substantially changed observed performance. Prediction-time availability matters as much as the choice of model.

03

Make trade-offs explicit

Useful detection requires balancing missed risks with false alerts that consume investigators’ time.

A credible risk model starts with leakage-safe validation and inputs that are genuinely available at prediction time.

05 / SCOPE & LIMITATIONS

What the evidence does—and doesn’t—say.

The saved notebook includes a deployment artifact selected with a potentially leaking feature. This is an academic case study, not a validated production AML system. Experimental scores are not presented as deployable performance.
